FrMS88-de1882-d1e111.summary: Poses the third question: whether the subject of the first complex principle has the same formal notion in God and creature according to the sermocinal sciences. The negative argument cites Dionysius: God is praised by us through the removal of all notions.
claims: Dionysius seems to deny any common notion between God and creatures.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e124.summary: Gives the contrary from Dionysius (ch. 4): as the sun communicates its light, God communicates his being. Then sets out four things in the soul — power, act, habit, and representative species — from which to argue, beginning with the power: one power has one first and adequate object, and the intellective power is one.
claims: God communicates his being as the sun its light.
One power has one first adequate object; the intellect is one power.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e146.summary: Argument from habit: supposing being is the subject of metaphysics, no science can demonstrate anything except through its proper subject or its notion; but metaphysics demonstrates things of God and creature, so being has a common notion.
claims: Metaphysics demonstrates of God and creatures through the common notion of being.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e155.summary: Rejects the evasion that there are two metaphysics, one in itself and one for us: however posited, a science cannot exceed its subject, and metaphysics for us still proves things of God through being, so we have a common concept.
claims: Even a metaphysics 'for us' proves things of God through a common concept of being.
concepts: metaphysics in se and quoad nos

FrMS88-de1882-d1e169.summary: Argument from the act of understanding: no act of understanding can of itself lead to knowledge of any term in which the notion of its first object is not contained; the philosophers had knowledge of God.
claims: Philosophers' natural knowledge of God requires that God fall under the first object of the intellect.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e176.summary: Argument from the representative: whatever causes a concept of something must contain it virtually or formally; the representative causes in us a concept of God.
claims: What causes a concept must contain its object virtually or formally.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e185.summary: Completes the argument: the created representative cannot contain anything in God virtually, being less noble, so it contains it formally. Then argues grammatically: a comparative presupposes the same formal notion in the positive (as 'whiter' requires whiteness in both); God is more a being than a creature, so being is formally in both.
claims: A created representation contains the concept of God formally, not virtually.
Comparison of degrees presupposes the same formal notion in the positive.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e205.summary: Further: as the comparative presupposes the positive, the superlative presupposes the comparative under the same notion; God is the supreme being.
claims: 'Supreme being' presupposes a common notion of being.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e212.summary: Further: whatever belongs to God alone belongs to him without comparative or superlative degree; conversely, what belongs to him in such degrees is not his alone; being is of this kind, so it belongs formally to God and creature.
claims: Predicates said of God in comparative degree are not proper to God.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e223.summary: Argument from reduplication: when whatever belongs to one 'inasmuch as such' belongs to the other 'inasmuch as such', they share one formal notion, since reduplication bears on the formal notion; whatever belongs to God inasmuch as being belongs to creature, and conversely.
claims: Reduplication bears on the formal notion, so shared reduplicative predicates imply a shared notion.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e242.summary: Second reduplication argument: when whatever is repugnant to one as such is repugnant to the other as such, they are of the same formal notion; to God and creature, as being, only nothing is repugnant.
claims: Only nothing is repugnant to being as such, whether in God or creature.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e255.summary: Argument from division: what is divided by dividing notions or differences has one formal notion; being is divided into God and creature by limited and unlimited.
claims: Being is divided into God and creature by the differences limited and unlimited.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e264.summary: States the possible reply that this is a division of a word into its significates.
concepts: division of a word into significates

FrMS88-de1882-d1e269.summary: Rejects the reply: every division of a word into significates is conventional and immediate, whereas this division is mediated.
claims: The division of being into God and creature is not conventional and is mediated.
concepts: division of a word into significates

FrMS88-de1882-d1e276.summary: Argument from definition: when something is defined by a common element and a contracting one, the common element belongs to something to which the contracting element does not; creature is defined by being and a contracting element, which is repugnant only to God; so being belongs to God.
claims: Creature is defined by being plus a contracting element that is repugnant only to God.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e289.summary: Argument from distribution: no equivocal term can be distributed ('every dog runs' is improper), but being can be.
claims: Equivocal terms cannot be distributed; being can.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e297.summary: Argument from contradiction: equivocal propositions have no contradictory ('every dog runs' and 'this dog does not run' do not contradict), but 'every being is limited' is contradicted by 'this being, God, is not limited'.
claims: Propositions about being admit genuine contradiction, unlike equivocal ones.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e308.summary: Argument from syllogism: 'every being is good; God is a being; so God is good' and the same for creature are good syllogisms. Either the middle term is the same in both — so it is said of God and creature by the same notion — or different, in which case the major would have to be distinguished, which is false since this is a metaphysical demonstration.
claims: Metaphysical syllogisms about God and creatures share a single middle term, being.

FrMS88-de1882-d1e328.summary: Reply to the opening argument: Dionysius' removal of all notions is true of the proper notions of creatures, not of the general ones.
claims: Dionysius' negations remove the proper, not the general, notions of creatures.

FrMS88-de1882.summary: The third question of the prologue asks whether the subject of the first complex principle (being) has the same formal notion (ratio formalis) in God and creature, approached through the sermocinal sciences and the faculties of the soul. Against Dionysius' praise of God by removal of all notions, Meyronnes argues from the four things in the soul — power, habit, act, and representative species: one power has one first adequate object; metaphysics, as a single science, demonstrates of God and creature through its proper subject (and the evasion of two metaphysics, in itself and for us, fails); the philosophers' act of knowing could lead to God only if God is contained in its first object; and a created representation must contain the divine notion formally since it cannot contain it virtually. He then gives a battery of grammatical and logical arguments: comparative and superlative degrees ('God is more a being', 'the supreme being') presuppose the same positive notion; reduplication ('inasmuch as being') shows whatever belongs to or is repugnant to one belongs to or is repugnant to the other; being is divided into God and creature by contracting differences (finite/infinite), which is not a division of a word into its meanings; creature is defined by being plus a contracting element; being can be distributed, and equivocal terms cannot; universal propositions about being have contradictories; and syllogisms in metaphysics have a single middle term. He replies that Dionysius' removals concern the proper, not the general, notions of creatures.
claims: Being has the same formal notion in God and creatures.
The single intellectual power, the single science of metaphysics, the natural act of knowing God, and the representative species all require a common formal notion of being.
Comparative and superlative predications of being presuppose a common positive notion.
Being is divided into God and creature by contracting differences, not as a word into its significates.
Being is distributable and enters genuine contradiction and syllogism, which equivocal terms cannot.
Dionysius' negations remove the proper notions of creatures, not the general ones.
